items.text: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.
Communicate clearly to users what the system’s state is — no action with consequences to users should be taken without informing them.
Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon.
Ensure that users can understand meaning without having to go look up a word’s definition.
Never assume your understanding of words or concepts will match that of your users.
Make sure the exit is clearly labeled and discoverable.
Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing.
Avoid slips by providing helpful constraints and good defaults.
The user should not have to remember information from one part of the interface to another.
Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed.
Ensure that the visual elements of the interface support the user's primary goals.
Keep the content and visual design of UI focused on the essentials.
Don't let unnecessary elements distract users from the information they really need.
Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
Use traditional error-message visuals, like bold, red text.
Tell users what went wrong in language they will understand — avoid technical jargon.
Keep it concise, and list concrete steps that need to be carried out.
Ensure that the help documentation is easy to search.
Aim for Inline Validation Whenever Possible
Keep Error Messages Next to Fields
Use Color to Differentiate Errors from Normal Field States
Use Modals or Confirmation Dialogs Sparingly
Don’t Validate Fields Before Input is Complete
Don’t Use Validation Summaries as the Only Indication of an Error
Don’t Use Tooltips to Report Errors
In these cases, make sure error messages are clear, actionable, and easy to locate when the form or page is reloaded.
However, don’t go overboard with success indicators.
Success indicators shouldn’t distract users from filling out forms and should only be used when the additional context helps complete the form faster or more accurately.
The message should follow error-message guidelines: it should be explicit, human-readable, polite, precise, and give constructive advice.
Make sure that the validation text stands out from the rest of the form so the user will notice it quickly.
However, don’t abuse animation: several animated icons can be overwhelming if there are multiple errors.
And don’t animate text — animated error messages are hard to read.
In most cases, avoid showing an error until the user has finished with the field and moved to the next field.
Ensure that users can easily detect errors, understand how to fix them, and see the error message while correcting the corresponding error.
Error messages must present themselves noticeably and recognizably to users.
Use noticeable, redundant, and accessible indicators.
Remember accessibility guidelines to aid the roughly 350 million people worldwide with a color-vision deficiency, and never use exclusively color or animation to indicate errors.
Don't assume that exploratory interactions (like the user moving text focus from a text box without filling it in) are errors.
However, do consider inline, real-time errors for error-prone interactions where users are unlikely to enter the correct information on their first try.
Error messages cannot rely on visuals alone.
They must contain copy to elaborate and assist the user with recovering from the error.
Error messages should be plainspoken using legible and readable text (many writing apps can give you feedback on a message's readability).
Avoid technical jargon and use language familiar to your users instead.
Hide or minimize the use of obscure error codes or abbreviations; show them for technical diagnostic purposes only.
Take a positive tone and don't blame the user.
Don't use phrasing that blames users or implies they are doing something wrong, such as invalid, illegal, or incorrect.
Avoid humor since it can become stale if users encounter the error frequently.
Offer accelerators to resolve the situation or share a bit of instruction to aid users' understanding and hopefully avoid the problem in the future.
For example, instead of just saying City and ZIP code don't match, let users click on a button for the city that matches the ZIP code they entered.
If additional information is required, use hypertext links to connect a concise error message to a page with supplementary material or an explanation of the problem.
